label: ENP
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{ENP}
	We say that a bounded domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb R^n$ satisfies the
	\emph{Enhanced Neumann P\'olya inequality} (the \emph{\ref{ENP} inequality} for short)
	if there exist positive constants $C_1(\Omega)$ and
	$C_2(\Omega)$ such that 
	\[
	\mathcal{N}_\Omega^N(\lambda) \ge
	L_{0,n}|\Omega|\lambda^{\frac n2}
	+ 	\max\left( 	C_1(\Omega)\lambda^{\frac{n-1}2}, C_2(\Omega) \right), \qquad \forall \lambda>0.
	\]
head: environment

label: general
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{general}
	Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ be a bounded domain satisfying the \ref{ENP} inequality, and let $U\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ be a bounded domain with smooth boundary. Then there exists a constant $a_0>0$, depending only on $\Omega$ and $U$, such that, for every $a\in(0,a_0)$ and every $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$ satisfying $\overline{x+aU}\subset\Omega$,  
	the domain 
	\[
	\Omega'=\Omega\setminus\overline{x+aU}
	\]
	also satisfies the \ref{ENP} inequality. In particular, the Neumann eigenvalues of $\Omega'$ satisfy P\'olya's conjecture.
head: environment

label: AssDiri
title: Remark
head: environment

label: mthm
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{mthm}
    Let $\Omega\subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be a bounded domain satisfying the \ref{ENP} inequality. For any $M\in\mathbb{Z}_+$, let $\{Q_i\}_{i=1}^M$ be a family of pairwise disjoint open cubes whose closures are contained in $\Omega$. Then there exist positive constants $A(M,\Omega)$ and $V(M,\Omega)$ such that, if
    \[
    \mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{Q}}:=\sum_{k=1}^M \ell(Q_k)^{n-1}<A(M,\Omega),\qquad
    \mathcal{V}_{\mathcal{Q}}:=\sum_{k=1}^M \ell(Q_k)^n<V(M,\Omega),
    \]
    the Neumann Laplacian eigenvalues of
    \[\Omega'=\Omega\setminus \overline{\cup_{k=1}^M Q_k}\]
    satisfy P\'olya's conjecture.
head: environment

title: Definition
head: environment

label: strip
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{strip}
	Every strip-tiling domain satisfies the \ref{ENP} inequality. Moreover, for a strip-tiling domain with  $w=\pi$,  the constants in the \ref{ENP} inequality can be chosen as 
	\[
	C_1(\Omega)=\frac{\left(4-\pi\right)L_{0,n-1}}{4\pi}|\Omega|, \qquad 
	C_2(\Omega) = 	\min\left( 	\frac12, \frac{\left(4-\pi\right)|\Omega|^{\frac1n}}{2\sqrt\pi}
	L_{0,n-1} 	\right).
	\]
head: environment

label: cor:strip
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:strip}
	Let $\Omega$ be a strip-tiling domain tiling
	$\mathbb{R}^{n-1}\times(0,\pi)$.
	For any $M\in\mathbb{Z}_+$, let
	$\{Q_i\}_{i=1}^M$
	be a family of pairwise disjoint open cubes whose closures are contained in $\Omega$, 
	such that 
	\[
	\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{Q}} \le \frac{(4-\pi)|\Omega|\pi^{n-2}L_{0,n-1}}{16n}.
	\] 
	Then every Neumann eigenvalue of $\Omega'=\Omega\setminus \overline{\cup_{k=1}^M Q_k}$ with 
	\[
	\mu_k(\Omega') >  \left( \frac{8\pi M}{(4-\pi)|\Omega|L_{0,n-1}} \right)^{\frac{2}{n-1}}
	\]
	satisfies P\'olya's inequality.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: The lower bound on $\mu_k(\Omega')$ is needed here because the proof of Theorem~\ref{mthm} relies on an explicit $L^\infty$ estimate for Neumann eigenfunctions (see \eqref{Linftybd}). While such an estimate is available in general, no explicit upper bound for the corresponding constant is currently known for strip-tiling domains. Thus Corollary \ref{cor:strip} reduces P\'olya's conjecture to verifying P\'olya's inequality for the finitely many eigenvalues below the explicit threshold above.

label: gentile
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{gentile}
	Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ be a bounded Lipschitz domain with $n\ge4$. Let
	$U\subset\mathbb{R}^{n_1}$ be a bounded Lipschitz domain,  where
	$2\le n_1\le n-2$, and set $n_2=n-n_1\ge2$.
	Suppose that $\Omega$ tiles $U\times\mathbb{R}^{n_2}$.
	Then $\Omega$ satisfies the \ref{ENP} inequality.

label: prop1
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop1}
    Let $\Omega=\Omega_1\times\Omega_2$ be a bounded domain in $\mathbb{R}^n$, where $\Omega_1\subset\mathbb{R}^{n_1}$ and $\Omega_2\subset\mathbb{R}^{n_2}$ with $n_1\ge 2$ and $n=n_1+n_2$. Assume that $\Omega_2$ has Lipschitz boundary. If $\Omega_1$ satisfies the Neumann part of P\'olya's conjecture, then $\Omega$ satisfies the \ref{ENP} inequality.
head: environment

label: prop2
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop2}
	Let $\Omega_1\subset\mathbb{R}^{n_1}$ and $\Omega_2\subset\mathbb{R}^{n_2}$ be bounded domains with $n_2\ge2$ and $n=n_1+n_2$. Assume that $\Omega_1$ has Lipschitz boundary and $\Omega_2$ has smooth boundary. Then there exists a constant $a_0>0$, depending on $\Omega_1$ and $\Omega_2$, such that for all $a\in(0,a_0)$, $a\Omega_1\times\Omega_2$ satisfies the \ref{ENP} inequality.

label: tile
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{tile}
	Let $\Omega,\Omega'\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ be bounded domains. If $\Omega$ satisfies the \ref{ENP} inequality and $\Omega'$ tiles $\Omega$, then $\Omega'$ also satisfies the \ref{ENP} inequality.

label: upbdIn
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{upbdIn}
	Let $I_n=(0,\pi)^n$. Then, for every $\lambda>0$,
	\[
	\mathcal{N}_{I_n}^N(\lambda)
	\le
	L_{0,n}\pi^n\lambda^{\frac n2}
	+
	\max\left(2n\lambda^{\frac{n-1}{2}},1\right).
	\]
head: environment

label: eq:decomposition
title: Proof
body_md:
Decomposing a nonnegative lattice point according to its set of nonzero coordinates gives
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:decomposition}
		\mathcal{N}_{I_n}^N(\lambda)
		=
		\sum_{j=0}^n\binom{n}{j}A_j(\sqrt{\lambda}),
	\end{equation}
	where $A_0(r):=1$ and for $j\ge1$, 
	\[
	A_j(r)
	:=	\#\left\{m\in\mathbb Z_{>0}^j:\ |m|<r\right\}
	\le  \frac{\omega_j}{2^j}r^j.
	\]
	Here $\omega_j$ denotes the volume of the
	unit ball in $\mathbb R^j$.  
	
	First suppose  $\lambda \ge 4$. 
	                  
	Then $\frac{{\sqrt \lambda}^j}{2^j}\le	2^{1-n}\lambda^{\frac{n-1}2}$ for  $0\le j\le n-1$, and thus 
	\[
	\mathcal{N}_{I_n}^N(\lambda)
	\le 	\sum_{j=0}^{n}
	\binom{n}{j}\frac{\omega_j}{2^j}\sqrt{\lambda}^j
	\le 	\frac{\omega_n}{2^n}\lambda^{\frac n2}+
	2^{1-n}\lambda^{\frac{n-1}2}
	\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\binom{n}{j}\omega_j.
	\]	 
	So the desired inequality follows from the fact 
	$\frac{\omega_n}{2^n} = L_{0,n}\pi^n$ 
	and 
	\[
	2^{1-n} \sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\binom{n}{j}\omega_j
	\le 2^{1-n} \left( 1+2\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}j\binom{n}{j}
	\right) 
	=\left( 2n+(1-2n)2^{1-n} \right) \le 2n,
	\]
	where we used the trivial identity $\omega_j \le 2j$ and the combinatorial identity 	
	\[ \sum_{j=1}^{n-1}j\binom{n}{j}=\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}n\binom{n-1}{j-1}=n(2^{n-1}-1).\] 
	
	It remains to consider $0<\lambda<4$. Since  
	\[
	\mathcal{N}_{I_n}^N(\lambda)
	=\begin{cases}
		1, & 0<\lambda \le 1,\\
		n+1, & 1 < \lambda \le 2, \\
		\frac{n^2+n+2}{2}, & 2 < \lambda \le 3, \\
		\frac{n^3+5n+6}{6}, & 3 < \lambda \le 4,
	\end{cases}
	\]
	the desired inequality holds for $0<\lambda \le 1$ trivially, and it is not hard to verify for $\lambda \in (k,k+1]$, where $k=1,2,3$, that 
	\[ 
	\mathcal{N}_{I_n}^N(\lambda) \le 	2n k^{\frac{n-1}2} \le 2n\lambda^{\frac{n-1}2}.
	\]
	This completes the proof.

label: lwsquare
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: eq:square-points
title: Proof
body_md:
We first prove the assertion for $\gamma=\frac12$, in which case $L_{\gamma,1}=\frac 14$.  
	If $0<\lambda\le1$, the desired inequality holds trivially. 
	To prove that the same inequality holds for all $\lambda>1$, we consider, on each interval $(k^2,(k+1)^2]$, $k\ge1$, the function
	\[
	f_k(\lambda)
	:=\sum_{i=0}^{k}\sqrt{\lambda-i^2}
	-\frac{\pi}{4}\lambda-\left(1-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\sqrt\lambda =\frac{\pi}4 \sqrt \lambda+\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sqrt{\lambda-i^2}
	-\frac{\pi}{4}\lambda.
	\]
	It is concave and thus its minimum is attained at an endpoint. So it
	suffices to verify $f_k(k^2) \ge 0$ and $f_k((k+1)^2) \ge 0$ for all $k$, or equivalently, to prove 
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:square-points}
		\sum_{i=0}^{k}
		\sqrt{k^2-i^2}
		-\frac{\pi}{4}k^2 \ge \left(1-\frac{\pi}{4}\right) k,
		\qquad k\in\mathbb N.
	\end{equation}
	
	Write
	$g_k(x)=\sqrt{k^2-x^2}$ on $[0,k]$.  Since
	$\int_0^k g_k(x)\,dx=\pi k^2/4$,                                 
	\begin{align*}
		\sum_{i=0}^{k}
		\sqrt{k^2-i^2}
		-\frac{\pi}{4}k^2
		&=\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}
		\left(g_k(i)-\int_i^{i+1}g_k(x)\,dx\right) \\
		&\ge \frac12\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}
		\frac{i}{\sqrt{k^2-i^2}} \\
		&\ge \frac12\int_0^{k-1}
		\frac{x}{\sqrt{k^2-x^2}}\,dx
		=\frac12\left(k-\sqrt{2k-1}\right).
	\end{align*}
    This gives \eqref{eq:square-points} for $k\ge 6$.
                
   
                      
                      
                  
   
   
	For $k=1,\dots,5$, direct computation shows that the difference
	between the left-hand side and the right-hand side of
	\eqref{eq:square-points} equals 
	\[
	0,\quad
	\sqrt3-\frac\pi2,\quad
	2\sqrt2+\sqrt5-\frac{3\pi}{2},\quad
	\sqrt{15}+2\sqrt3+\sqrt7-3\pi,\quad
	2\sqrt6+\sqrt{21}+7-5\pi
	\]
	respectively, all of which are nonnegative.  This proves the lemma for $\gamma=1/2$. 
	
	Now let $\gamma>\frac12$.  The beta-integral identity
	\[
	(\lambda-i^2)^\gamma
	=
	\mathscr{B}\left(\frac32,\gamma-\frac12\right)^{-1}
	\int_0^\infty
	(\lambda-i^2-t)_+^{\frac 12}
	\,t^{\gamma-\frac32}\,dt,
	\]
	and the already proved endpoint case yield
	\begin{align*}
		 \sum_{i\in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0},i^2<\lambda}\!(\lambda-i^2)^\gamma  
		 =&\mathscr{B}\left(\frac32,\gamma-\frac12\right)^{-1}\int_0^\infty \sum_{i\in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0},i^2<\lambda}(\lambda-i^2-t)_+^{\frac 12}t^{\gamma-\frac32}\mathrm dt\\
		\ge&\mathscr{B}\left(\frac32,\gamma-\frac12\right)^{-1}\!\int_0^\infty\! \left(\frac\pi4 (\lambda\!-\!t)_++\left(1\!-\!\frac{\pi}{4}\right)(\lambda\!-\!t)_+^{\frac 12}\right)t^{\gamma-\frac32}\mathrm dt\\
		=&L_{\gamma,1}\pi\lambda^{\gamma+\frac12}+\left(1-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\lambda^\gamma.
	\end{align*}

label: lwbdR2
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lwbdR2}
	For all $\lambda>0$, we have
	\[
	\mathcal{N}^N_\mathcal{R}(\lambda)
	\ge
	L_{0,n}|\mathcal{R}|\lambda^{\frac n2}
	+
	\max\left(
	\left(1-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)
	L_{0,n-1}|\widetilde\mathcal{R}|
	\lambda^{\frac{n-1}{2}},
	\left(1-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)
	L_{0,n-1}|\widetilde\mathcal{R}|
	\right).
	\]
head: environment

label: new
title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\widetilde\mathcal{R}$ satisfies P\'olya's conjecture, for all $\lambda>0$,
	\[
	\begin{aligned}
		\mathcal{N}^N_{\mathcal{R}}(\lambda)
		=
		\sum_{i\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0},\,i^2<\lambda}
		\mathcal{N}^N_{\widetilde\mathcal{R}}(\lambda-i^2)
		\ge
		L_{0,n-1}|\widetilde\mathcal{R}|
		\sum_{i\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0},\,i^2<\lambda}
		(\lambda-i^2)^{\frac{n-1}2}.
	\end{aligned}
	\]
	Applying Lemma~\ref{lwsquare} and \eqref{Cd1d2} gives
	\begin{equation}\label{new}
		\begin{aligned}
			\mathcal{N}^N_{\mathcal{R}}(\lambda)
			&\ge
			L_{0,n-1}|\widetilde\mathcal{R}|
			\left(
			L_{\frac{n-1}{2},1}\pi
			\lambda^{\frac n2}
			+
			\left(1-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)
			\lambda^{\frac{n-1}{2}}
			\right)\\
			&=
			L_{0,n}|\mathcal{R}|\lambda^{\frac n2}
			+
			\left(1-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)
			L_{0,n-1}|\widetilde\mathcal{R}|
			\lambda^{\frac{n-1}{2}}.
		\end{aligned}
	\end{equation}
	
	It remains to consider $0<\lambda\leq1$. Since
	$\mathcal{N}^N_{\mathcal{R}}(\lambda)=1$, we have for all $0<\lambda\leq1$,
	\[ \mathcal{N}^N_{\mathcal{R}}(\lambda) - L_{0,n}|\mathcal{R}|\lambda^{\frac n2} \ge 1-L_{0,n}|\mathcal{R}|.
	\]
	For simplicity, write 
	\[
	A_n=L_{0,n}\pi^n.
	\]
	Since $A_{n+2}=A_n\frac{\pi}{2n+4} <A_n,$ 
	we have
	\begin{equation}\label{ineqAn}
		\sup_{n\geq1}A_n
		\leq
		\max(A_1,A_2)=1,
		\qquad
		\sup_{n\geq2}A_n
		\leq
		\max(A_2,A_3)=\frac{\pi}{4}.
	\end{equation}
	Moreover,
	\[
	L_{0,n}|\mathcal{R}|\leq A_n,
	\qquad
	L_{0,n-1}|\widetilde\mathcal{R}|\leq A_{n-1}.
	\]
	Hence, for every $n\geq2$,
	\[
		\left(1-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)
		L_{0,n-1}|\widetilde\mathcal{R}|
		\leq
		\left(1-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)A_{n-1}
		\leq
		1-\frac{\pi}{4}
		\leq
		1-A_n
		\le
		1-L_{0,n}|\mathcal{R}|.
	\]
	Consequently, for all $0<\lambda\leq1$,
	\[
	\mathcal{N}^N_{\mathcal{R}}(\lambda)
	\ge
	L_{0,n}|\mathcal{R}|\lambda^{\frac n2}
	+
	\left(1-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)
	L_{0,n-1}|\widetilde\mathcal{R}|.
	\]
	
	For $\lambda\geq1$, the desired result follows from
	\eqref{new}, since $\lambda^{\frac{n-1}{2}}\geq1$. Combining
	this with the preceding estimate completes the proof.

name: Strict Blichfeldt lemma for Euclidean balls

label: lem:periodic-plane-waves
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For every nonzero $\zeta\in\Gamma^*$, we have 
	\[ 
	\int_C e^{i\zeta\cdot x}\,dx=0.
	\]
	As a result, given any $\theta$, the restrictions to $C$ of
	\[
	u_{\xi,\theta}(x):=e^{i(\xi+\theta)\cdot x},\qquad \xi\in\Gamma^*,
	\]
	are pairwise orthogonal in $L^2(C)$.  They also diagonalize the Dirichlet form on their span:
	\[
	\int_C\nabla u_{\xi,\theta}\cdot
	\overline{\nabla u_{\eta,\theta}}\,dx
	=|\xi+\theta|^2|C|\,\delta_{\xi\eta}.
	\]
	The conclusion follows from the standard min-max principle.

label: lem:periodic-strict
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Strict P\'olya for periodic tilings

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $\lambda>0$ and put $r=\sqrt\lambda$.  For the dual lattice one has $ \operatorname{covol}(\Gamma^*)=\frac{(2\pi)^n}{|C|}.$ 
	Therefore, by \cref{lem:strict-blichfeldt-ball}, some shift $\theta$ satisfies
	\[
	\#\{\xi\in\Gamma^*:|\xi+\theta|^2<\lambda\}\!\ge\! \left[\frac{|B_r||C|}{(2\pi)^n}+1\right]\!>\! \frac{|B_r||C|}{(2\pi)^n}=\frac{\omega_n\lambda^{n/2}|C|}{(2\pi)^n} 
	=\ell L_{0,n}|\Omega|\lambda^{\frac n2}.
	\]
	Combining this with \cref{lem:periodic-plane-waves} yields
	\[
	\ell N_\Omega^N(\lambda)> \ell L_{0,n}|\Omega|\lambda^{\frac n2},
	\]
	and hence the strict P\'olya inequality.

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\Omega=\Omega_1\times\Omega_2$, the Neumann eigenvalues of $\Omega$ are
\[
\mu_i(\Omega_1)+\mu_j(\Omega_2),\qquad i,j\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}.
\]
Thus, for any $\lambda>0$, under the assumption that $\Omega_1$ satisfies P\'olya's conjecture, 
\[
\mathcal{N}^N_{\Omega}(\lambda)=\sum_{j:\mu_j(\Omega_2)<\lambda} \mathcal{N}^N_{\Omega_1}(\lambda-\mu_j(\Omega_2))\ge L_{0,n_1}|\Omega_1|\sum_{j:\mu_j(\Omega_2)<\lambda}(\lambda-\mu_j(\Omega_2))^{\frac{n_1}2}.
\]
Then, by \eqref{FLRiesz}, as $\lambda\to\infty$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
	\mathcal{N}^N_{\Omega}(\lambda)
	=&L_{0,n_1}|\Omega_1|\left(L_{\frac{n_1}2,n_2}|\Omega_2|\lambda^{\frac{n}{2}}+\frac14L_{\frac{n_1}2,n_2-1}|\partial\Omega_2|\lambda^{\frac{n-1}{2}}+o(\lambda^{\frac{n-1}{2}})\right)\\
	=&L_{0,n}|\Omega|\lambda^{\frac{n}{2}}+\frac 14L_{0,n-1}|\Omega_1| |\partial\Omega_2|\lambda^{\frac{n-1}{2}}+o(\lambda^{\frac{n-1}{2}}).
\end{aligned}
\]
Hence, there exists $\Lambda(\Omega)>0$ such that for all $\lambda>\Lambda(\Omega)$,
\[
\mathcal{N}^N_{\Omega}(\lambda)\ge L_{0,n}|\Omega|\lambda^{\frac{n}{2}}+\frac 15 L_{0,n-1} |\Omega_1| |\partial\Omega_2|\lambda^{\frac{n-1}{2}}.
\] 
  
On the other hand, since $\frac{n_1}{2}\ge 1$, by Lemma \ref{rfofGJL} and the Aizenman--Lieb identity, for all $\lambda>0$,
\[
\mathcal{N}^N_{\Omega}(\lambda)>L_{0,n_1}|\Omega_1|L_{\frac{n_1}2,n_2}|\Omega_2|\lambda^{\frac{n}{2}}=L_{0,n}|\Omega|\lambda^{\frac{n}{2}}.
\]
Combining this with the large $\lambda$ asymptotics and the trivial lower bound $\mathcal{N}^N_\Omega(\lambda)\ge1$, there exist positive constants $C_1(\Omega),C_2(\Omega)$ such that for all $\lambda>0$,
\[
\mathcal{N}_\Omega^N(\lambda)\ge L_{0,n}|\Omega|\lambda^{\frac n2}+\max\left(C_1(\Omega)\lambda^{\frac{n-1}2},C_2(\Omega)\right).
\]
This verifies the \ref{ENP} inequality.

title: Proof
body_md:
The Neumann eigenvalues of $a\Omega_1\times\Omega_2$ are
\[
a^{-2}\mu_i(\Omega_1)+\mu_j(\Omega_2),\qquad i,j\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}.
\]
Hence,
\[
\mathcal{N}^N_{a\Omega_1\times\Omega_2}(\lambda)
=
\sum_{a^{-2}\mu_i(\Omega_1)<\lambda}
\mathcal{N}^N_{\Omega_2}(\lambda-a^{-2}\mu_i(\Omega_1)).
\]

By Lemma \ref{Seeasy}, there exists a constant $\alpha>0$ such that for all $\lambda>0$,
\[
\mathcal{N}^N_{\Omega_2}(\lambda)
\ge
L_{0,n_2}|\Omega_2|\lambda^{\frac{n_2}{2}}
-\alpha \lambda^{\frac{n_2-1}{2}}.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\begin{aligned}
	\mathcal{N}^N_{a\Omega_1\times\Omega_2}(\lambda)
	\ge&
	\,L_{0,n_2}|\Omega_2|a^{-n_2}
	\sum_{\mu_i(\Omega_1)<a^2\lambda}
	(a^2\lambda-\mu_i(\Omega_1))^{\frac{n_2}{2}}
	\\
	&
	-\alpha a^{1-n_2}
	\sum_{\mu_i(\Omega_1)<a^2\lambda}
	(a^2\lambda-\mu_i(\Omega_1))^{\frac{n_2-1}{2}}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Applying Lemma~\ref{FL3term} and \eqref{FLRiesz}, after choosing $a>0$
sufficiently small, there exist $\Lambda>0$ and $c>0$ such that for all $\lambda>a^{-2}\Lambda$,
\[
\mathcal{N}^N_{a\Omega_1\times\Omega_2}(\lambda)
\ge
L_{0,n}|a\Omega_1\times\Omega_2|
\lambda^{\frac n2}
+c\lambda^{\frac{n-1}2}.
\]

On the other hand, by \cite[Theorem~1.1]{HW24}, after possibly
decreasing $a$,  
\[
\mathcal{N}^N_{a\Omega_1\times\Omega_2}(\lambda)
>
L_{0,n}|a\Omega_1\times\Omega_2|
\lambda^{\frac n2}, \qquad \forall \lambda>0.
\]
Combining these estimates with the trivial bound $
\mathcal{N}^N_{a\Omega_1\times\Omega_2}(\lambda)\ge 1$, 
we conclude that there exist positive constants
$C_1(a\Omega_1\times\Omega_2)$ and
$C_2(a\Omega_1\times\Omega_2)$ such that
\[
\mathcal{N}^N_{a\Omega_1\times\Omega_2}(\lambda)
\ge
L_{0,n}|a\Omega_1\times\Omega_2|
\lambda^{\frac n2}
+\max\!\left(
C_1(a\Omega_1\times\Omega_2)\lambda^{\frac{n-1}2},
C_2(a\Omega_1\times\Omega_2)
\right).
\]
Hence the \ref{ENP} inequality holds.

label: eq:frequency-target-v3
title: Proof
body_md:
For simplicity, denote 
	\[
	a:=\frac5{1008},
	\qquad
	c:=\frac{269}{7840},
	\qquad
	x_*:=\frac{c}{a}=\frac{2421}{350}.
	\]
	We prove
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:frequency-target-v3}
		\mathcal N_\mathbb{D}^N(x^2) \geq \frac{x^2}{4}+\max(ax,c),
		\qquad x>0.
	\end{equation}
	
	First suppose \(x>x_*\). According to  \cite[(C.22)]{li2026p},
	for \(x\geq20/3\),
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:Li-C22-v3}
		\#\{j:\mu_j(\mathbb{D})\leq x^2\} 	> 	\frac{x^2}{4}
		+x\left(\frac{13}{40}-\frac1\pi\right)
		-\frac{13}{50\pi x}.
	\end{equation} 	
	Using the   lower bound
	\(\pi>3141592/10^6\), we obtain, for $x>x_*$, 
	\begin{align*}
		\frac{13}{40}-\frac1\pi-\frac{13}{50\pi x^2}
		>
		\frac{13}{40}
		-\left(1+\frac{13}{50x_*^2}\right)\frac{10^6}{3141592}
		=
		\frac{456690232967}{92068139178360}
		>
		a.
	\end{align*}     
	Since \(x_* >20/3\), we thus get
	\[
	\#\{j:\mu_j(\mathbb{D})\leq x^2\} 	>
	\frac{x^2}{4}+ax, \qquad x\geq x_*.
	\]
	As a result, for any $x>x_*$,
	\[
	\mathcal N_\mathbb{D}^N(x^2) \geq \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0+} 	\#\{j:\mu_j(\mathbb{D})\leq (x-\varepsilon)^2\} 
	\ge  	\frac{x^2}{4}+ax.
	\] 
	
	Next suppose \(0<x\leq x_*\).  As in the Rayleigh--Ritz construction of
	\cite[Section~4.3]{li2026p}, we set 
	\[
	V_{m,\ell}
	:=
	\operatorname{span}\{r^{p_0},\ldots,r^{p_{\ell-1}}\},
	\qquad
	p_i:=m+2i.
	\]
	In this basis, the quadratic-form and Gram matrices are
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:disk-ritz-matrices-v3}
		A_{ij}
		=
		\frac{p_ip_j+m^2}{p_i+p_j},
		\qquad
		B_{ij}
		=
		\frac1{p_i+p_j+2},
		\qquad
		0\leq i,j\leq\ell-1,
	\end{equation}
	with \(A_{00}:=0\) when \(m=0\); cf.~\cite[(4.9)]{li2026p}.
	The matrix \(B\) is positive definite.
	
	Let
	\(\theta^{(m,\ell)}_1\leq\cdots\leq
	\theta^{(m,\ell)}_\ell\)
	be the generalized eigenvalues of \(Av=\theta Bv\).  
	The min--max principle gives
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:ritz-minmax-v3}
		\lambda_{m,k}\leq\theta^{(m,\ell)}_k,
		\qquad 1\leq k\leq\ell.
	\end{equation}
	For a real symmetric matrix \(M\), let \(n_-(M)\) denote the
	number of its negative eigenvalues, counted with multiplicity.
	For every \(T\), Sylvester's law of inertia gives
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:inertia-counts-v3}
		n_-(A-TB)
		=
		\#\bigl\{k:\theta^{(m,\ell)}_k<T\bigr\}.
	\end{equation}
	
	For \(q\in\{1,3,5,6,8\}\), put
	\[
	T_q:=4(q-c).
	\]
	Thus \(T_q/4+c=q\). Exact rational
	\(LDL^{\mathsf T}\) elimination applied to
	\(A_{m,\ell}-T_qB_{m,\ell}\) gives the following pivots. The last
	column is the number of negative pivots and hence, by
	\eqref{eq:inertia-counts-v3}, the number of Ritz eigenvalues below
	\(T_q\).
	\[
	\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c}
		(m,\ell)&q&T_q&\text{diagonal pivots}&n_-
		\\ \hline
		(1,2)&1&\dfrac{7571}{1960}
		&\left(\dfrac{269}{7840},
		-\dfrac{95442359}{37961280}\right)&1
		\\[2mm]
		(2,2)&3&\dfrac{23251}{1960}
		&\left(\dfrac{269}{11760},
		-\dfrac{875514519}{84358400}\right)&1
		\\[2mm]
		(0,3)&5&\dfrac{38931}{1960}
		&\left(-\dfrac{38931}{3920},
		\dfrac{2703}{15680},
		-\dfrac{698796893}{1907236800}\right)&2
		\\[2mm]
		(3,2)&6&\dfrac{46771}{1960}
		&\left(\dfrac{269}{15680},
		-\dfrac{3249474359}{158172000}\right)&1
		\\[2mm]
		(4,2)&8&\dfrac{62451}{1960}
		&\left(\dfrac{15949}{19600},
		-\dfrac{866322013}{5251686720}\right)&1
		\\[2mm]
		(1,3)&8&\dfrac{62451}{1960}
		&\left(-\dfrac{54611}{7840},
		\dfrac{902174333}{2568901440},
		-\dfrac{11719249600621}{707304677072000}\right)&2
	\end{array}
	\]
	Combining \eqref{eq:ritz-minmax-v3} and
	\eqref{eq:inertia-counts-v3} therefore gives
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:finite-spectral-bounds-v3}
		\begin{aligned}
			(j'_{1,1})^2<T_1,
			\quad  
			(j'_{2,1})^2&<T_3,
			&
			(j'_{0,1})^2&<T_5,
			&
			(j'_{3,1})^2&<T_6,
			\\
			\max\bigl\{(j'_{4,1})^2,(j'_{1,2})^2\bigr\}&<T_8.
		\end{aligned}
	\end{equation}
	Indeed, in the \(m=0\) row the two Ritz values below \(T_5\)
	control \(\lambda_{0,2}=(j'_{0,1})^2\), since
	\(\lambda_{0,1}=0\); the last row similarly controls
	\(\lambda_{1,2}=(j'_{1,2})^2\). 
	Taking  multiplicities into account, the bounds in
	\eqref{eq:finite-spectral-bounds-v3} give
	\[
	\begin{array}{c|c}
		\text{range of \(x^2\)}
		&\text{lower bound for \(\mathcal N_\mathbb{D}^N(x^2)\)}
		\\ \hline
		0<x^2\leq T_1&1\\
		T_1<x^2\leq T_3&3\\
		T_3<x^2\leq T_5&5\\
		T_5<x^2\leq T_6&6\\
		T_6<x^2\leq T_8&8\\
		T_8<x^2\leq x_*^2&12.
	\end{array}
	\]
	In each of the first five rows, the displayed lower count is \(q\),
	and hence
	\[
	\frac{x^2}{4}+c
	\leq
	\frac{T_q}{4}+c=q.
	\]
	For the last row, an exact calculation gives
	\[
	\frac{x^2}{4}+c
	\leq
	\frac{x_*^2}{4}+c
	=
	12-\frac{3893}{980000}
	<12.
	\]
	Consequently,
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:low-frequency-v3}
		\mathcal N_\mathbb{D}^N(x^2) \geq \frac{x^2}{4}+c,
		\qquad 0<x\leq x_*.
	\end{equation}
	This finishes the proof of  \eqref{eq:frequency-target-v3} and hence  \eqref{eq:unit-disk-explicit-remainder-v3}.

label: lem:bessel-critical-value
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:bessel-critical-value}
	Let $a\ge 2n$ satisfies $J_n'(a)=0$, where for $n=0$ we further assume $a>0$, then
	$
	|J_n(a)|> \frac{1}{2\sqrt a}.
	$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Set
	\[
	u_n(x)=\sqrt{x}\,J_n(x),
	\qquad
	q_n(x)=1-\frac{n^2-\frac14}{x^2}.
	\]
	Then $u_n$ satisfies $u_n''+q_n(x)u_n=0$.  
	For $x\ge 2n$, we have $q_n(x)>0$ and $q_n'(x)>0$. Hence the Sonin function
	\[
	S_n(x):=u_n(x)^2+\frac{u_n'(x)^2}{q_n(x)}
	\]
	satisfies
	\[
	S_n'(x) = -\frac{q_n'(x)}{q_n(x)^2}u_n'(x)^2 \le 0.
	\]
	Moreover, by the standard asymptotics of $J_n$, 
	\[
	\lim_{x\to\infty}S_n(x)=\frac{2}{\pi}.
	\]
	Therefore $
	S_n(a)>\frac{2}{\pi}.$
	On the other hand,$J_n'(a)=0$ implies  $u_n'(a)=\frac{u_n(a)}{2a}$ and thus
	\[
	S_n(a) = aJ_n(a)^2 \left( 1 + \frac{1}{4\left(a^2-n^2+\frac14\right)} \right) < 2aJ_n(a)^2.
	\]
	So we get $
	2aJ_n(a)^2 >\frac{2}{\pi}$
	and consequently 
	\[
	|J_n(a)|>\frac 1{\sqrt{\pi a}}>\frac{1}{2\sqrt a}.
	\]

label: lem:bessel-near-turning
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:bessel-near-turning}
	Let \(n\geq1\), let \(a\) be a positive zero of \(J_n'\), and set
	\[
	M_n(a)=\max_{0\leq x\leq a}|J_n(x)|.
	\]
	Then
	\[
	\int_0^a xJ_n(x)^2\,dx
	\geq \frac{n}{4}M_n(a)^2.
	\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For \(x>n\), put
	\[
	p_n(x)=1-\frac{n^2}{x^2},
	\qquad
	S_n(x)=J_n(x)^2+\frac{J_n'(x)^2}{p_n(x)}.
	\]
	Using the Bessel equation, one obtains for \(x>n\),
	\[
	S_n'(x)
	=
	-\frac{2J_n'(x)^2}{x\,p_n(x)}
	-\frac{p_n'(x)J_n'(x)^2}{p_n(x)^2}
	\leq0.
	\]
	Thus the absolute values of the successive extrema of \(J_n\) are
	nonincreasing.  Since \(j'_{n,1}\) is the first positive critical point and $|J_n|$ is even,
	\[
	M_n(a)=J_n(j'_{n,1})=\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}}|J_n(x)|.
	\]
	
	By \eqref{eq:BesselFunctionInt}, $J_n$ is entire. Moreover, it is  of exponential type at most $1$ since 
	\[
	|J_n(z)|
	\leq
	\frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^\pi e^{|y||\sin\theta|}\,d\theta
	\leq e^{|y|}
	\leq e^{|z|}.
	\]
	Hence by Bernstein's inequality
	\cite{Bernstein1923}, 
	\[
	\|J_n'\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb R)}
	\leq
	\|J_n\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb R)}
	=M_n(a).
	\]
	As a consequence, for $x\in[j'_{n,1}-1,j'_{n,1}]$,  
	\[
	J_n(x)
	\geq J_n(j'_{n,1})-(j'_{n,1}-x)M_n(a)
	=(1-j'_{n,1}+x)M_n(a).
	\]
	Since \(j'_{n,1}\geq n\geq1\) and \(a\geq j'_{n,1}\), it follows that
	\begin{align*}
		\int_0^a\! xJ_n(x)^2\,dx
		\geq
		M_n(a)^2\int_{j'_{n,1}\!-\!1}^{j'_{n,1}}\! x(1\!-\!j'_{n,1}\!+\!x)^2\,dx=
		\frac{4j'_{n,1}\!-\!1}{12}M_n(a)^2\geq\frac{n}{4}M_n(a)^2.\!
	\end{align*}
